---
title: "Exercise: all smoothers on one image"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- name the belief behind each of eight smoothers and predict where it fails;
- recognise a method from what it does to a profile or from its method noise;
- choose a score that matches a question, and a method that matches an image;
- *(math)* classify the methods as linear or not, convex or not, local or not.

## Background

| method | belief | typical failure |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian (heat) | smooth | blurs every edge and fine detail |
| median | outliers rare, structures wider than the window | removes thin lines and dots |
| Perona–Malik | piecewise smooth, edges above $K$ | staircases ramps, keeps spikes |
| TV | piecewise constant | staircases, lowers small-object contrast, flattens texture |
| bilateral | nearby similar values belong together | fails when noise ≈ edge height; noisy rim at edges |
| non-local means | the image repeats | no help on unique details |
| wavelet shrinkage | few large coefficients | ringing near edges, loses medium-size texture |
| Wiener | known power spectrum | blurs sharp, sparse structures like a Gaussian |

## By hand

**B1.** **Match the profile.** A row with a step, a ramp, a 1-pixel line and a soft step, smoothed by six methods. Which method made each description?
(a) Step and line slightly blurred, ramp smooth, everything a little noisy.
(b) Step sharp, line gone completely, ramp smooth.
(c) Step sharp, line kept, ramp turned into a few terraces.
(d) Step sharp, line kept, a soft step made sharper, flat parts very clean after many repetitions.
(e) Everything sharp and clean, except a unique feature that is as noisy as before.
(f) Small ripples (overshoots) next to the step.

**B2.** **Choose and justify** (name the belief): (a) a crystal lattice in electron microscopy; (b) a segmentation map that is nearly piecewise constant (a few flat regions); (c) tissue with smooth intensity gradients; (d) an image with hot pixels.

**B3.** Two methods give the same PSNR on a test card. You will count small spots of radius 2–3. Which scores do you compare? Which tab of the demo shows the answer at a glance?

**B4.** After smoothing you threshold the image to find cells, and then report each cell's integrated intensity. On which image do you threshold, and on which do you integrate? Why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) Gaussian (or Wiener): linear blur at a small σ. (b) Median: keeps steps, removes structures thinner than the window. (c) TV (or Perona–Malik with $K$ below the ramp's slope): staircasing. (d) Iterated bilateral (or long Perona–Malik): cartoon, backward-diffusion-like sharpening. (e) Non-local means: the unique feature has no copies. (f) Wavelet shrinkage (or Wiener): oscillations near a step from removed high-frequency or detail coefficients.

**B2.** (a) Non-local means: the image repeats itself. (b) TV: piecewise constant with short boundaries. (c) Gaussian, Wiener or a gentle Perona–Malik with large $K$: the image is smooth; TV would staircase the gradients. (d) Median: outliers are rare and isolated.

**B3.** The contrast kept for small discs ("disc kept") and the method noise around small objects; also the edge width if spot size matters. The **scores** tab gives the numbers, the **method noise** tab shows whether the spots appear in what was removed.

**B4.** Threshold on the smoothed (preferably edge-preserving) image: cleaner masks. Integrate on the raw image inside the masks: every smoother moves intensity between objects and their surroundings (TV lowers small-object contrast at rate perimeter/area, Gaussians spread it out), while the raw image is an unbiased, if noisy, measurement.
:::

### Math questions

**B5.** *(math)* Classify the eight methods as linear or non-linear, as minimising a convex energy, a non-convex one or no energy, and as local or non-local. Give a one-line reason each.

**B6.** *(math)* Soft thresholding of a coefficient $c$ with threshold $t$ minimises $\tfrac12(x - c)^2 + t|x|$. Show this, and explain why with an orthogonal wavelet transform $W$ it minimises $\tfrac12\|Wu - Wy\|^2 + t\|Wu\|_1$ for the whole image.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B5.** Gaussian: linear (a convolution), convex (one implicit heat step = quadratic smoothing), local. Median: non-linear (order statistic), convex per window (minimises $\sum|I_q - m|$), local. Perona–Malik: non-linear, non-convex energy (flattening penalty), local. TV: non-linear, convex (ROF), local. Bilateral: non-linear (weights depend on the image), no single convex energy (one reweighting step of a robust, flattening penalty), local. NLM: non-linear, no energy (one heat step on a graph built from the image), non-local. Wavelet shrinkage: non-linear (thresholding), convex ($\ell_1$ on coefficients), local in space and scale. Wiener: linear, convex (minimum mean squared error among linear filters), global (it acts on the whole spectrum).

**B6.** For $x > 0$ the derivative is $x - c + t$, zero at $x = c - t$ (valid if $c > t$); for $x < 0$, $x = c + t$ (valid if $c < -t$); otherwise the minimum is at the kink $x = 0$ (the subgradient $[-t, t]$ contains $c$). So $x = \mathrm{sign}(c)\max(|c| - t, 0)$. With $W$ orthogonal, $\|Wu - Wy\|^2 = \|u - y\|^2$, and the energy separates into one such problem per coefficient: thresholding each coefficient minimises the whole.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

The test card (or the micrograph) with seeded Gaussian, Poisson or salt-and-pepper noise, smoothed by all eight methods, each started at its best-PSNR setting for the preset noise levels (they compute one after the other). Click a result to select it; its parameter slider is in the panel ("back to best PSNR" resets). Tabs: results (with a synchronised 40 × 40 **zoom**), method noise, profiles along row 112, and scores (best per column in green). **Threshold** marks the pixels above 120.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="smoothercompare" data-preset="g15" data-tab="scores"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/smoothercompare.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **Gaussian noise, moderate**, scores tab. Which method keeps the 1-pixel line best among those with a PSNR of at least 30 dB? Which keeps the small disc best?

**E2.** Presets **salt and pepper** and **Poisson, few photons**. Which method wins the PSNR in each? Look at the method noise of the median for salt and pepper.

**E3.** Preset **strong noise: all fail differently** (σn = 40). Rank the methods by PSNR. Then look at the results tab: describe how three of them fail.

**E4.** Presets **texture: NLM** and **piecewise constant: TV** (zoomed). Which method looks best in each crop, and which looks worst?

**E5.** Preset **best PSNR vs best look** (micrograph, settings chosen by eye). Compare the PSNR with the best-PSNR settings (button "back to best PSNR"). Which would you show in a figure, and why?

**E6.** Preset **smoothing before thresholding** (σn = 40). Look at the red masks. Select TV and raise λ to about 45; select the Gaussian and raise σ to 2. Which mask is cleaner on the square and the discs?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Among PSNR ≥ 30 dB (TV 30.6, bilateral 30.1, NLM 34.6): bilateral and NLM keep the line fully (1.00), TV 0.85. The small disc (radius 3): the Gaussian keeps 0.98 of its contrast at its (very mild) best setting, Wiener 0.98, Perona–Malik 0.96; TV 0.88 (perimeter/area loss) and bilateral 0.86.

**E2.** Salt and pepper (5 %): the median wins (26.3 dB; NLM 25.1, Perona–Malik 24.2, Gaussian 23.5); its method noise shows the removed outliers and, unfortunately, the line and the lattice dots. Poisson (30 photons at 255): NLM 26.8, TV 25.9, Perona–Malik 25.4, Gaussian 24.4.

**E3.** NLM 24.6, TV 24.1, Perona–Malik 23.2, Gaussian 22.7, wavelets 22.7, bilateral 22.6, Wiener 22.6, median 21.5 dB. Typical failures: the Gaussian and Wiener leave blotchy noise and blurred edges; the median loses the line and the lattice; TV turns the noise in flat regions into patches and loses the smallest discs; NLM loses the unique ring and the rims of discs (no copies).

**E4.** Lattice crop: NLM gives clean, identical dots; TV and the median flatten or lose the dots; Gaussian and Wiener leave them blurry and noisy. Square crop: TV gives a flat interior with crisp edges and corners; NLM is nearly as good; the Gaussian and Wiener are noisy and soft.

**E5.** On the micrograph the best-PSNR settings give about 26.4 dB (Gaussian), 26.5 (TV), 26.2 (bilateral), 25.7 (NLM); the "by eye" settings 21.8, 24.3, 24.4, 23.3: lower PSNR, cleaner look. For a figure the stronger smoothing may be acceptable if stated; for analysis the less smoothed one loses less real structure. Neither replaces measuring on the raw image.

**E6.** At the best-PSNR settings all masks are speckled (they smooth too little for a threshold at σn = 40). With TV λ ≈ 45 the square and discs come out crisp with clean flat regions (105 wrong pixels in that part of the card, flat-region noise 2.0); with a Gaussian of σ = 2 the shapes are rounded and the smallest disc is lost (151 wrong, noise 4.7); Perona–Malik (time 2) is in between (132).
:::

## Where this leads

The day's methods all smooth with a hand-made belief. **Learned** denoisers (the deconvolution day's pointer in [denoise](../denoise/lec.qmd), and the generative-model days: [diffusion priors](../diffusion-inverse/lec.qmd)) learn the belief from data; they are judged with exactly the same tools as here: a test card with truth, method noise, feature scores, and the rule that measurements come from the raw image.

The [sparse representations day](../sparsity/lec.qmd), next, adds one more hand-made belief, "few large coefficients in a basis or a patch dictionary", and uses it beyond denoising: deblurring, inpainting and measuring less. Much later, heat flow returns inside a cell-segmentation network as its training target ([flow fields to objects](../cellpose/lec.qmd)).
